slides.say: x and y are integers. Given: three is smaller than x plus y, in absolute value. Which of the following is possible but not necessarily true?
Unlike the last few questions, this is a technique question. And before we start, let's understand the wording. Possible, but not necessarily true.

So anything that's never true is not possible, and it's out. And anything that's always true is necessarily true, so it's out too. We want the one that's sometimes true and sometimes not. [short pause] Two ways, the rules first, and then plugging in numbers.

[short pause] Our first method. Choice number one looks like the given, with brackets instead of bars, and a square. Both sides of the given are positive, so I'm allowed to square them. Why? Remember, with positive numbers, the bigger number also has the bigger square. Three squared, three times three, is nine.
And x plus y in absolute value, squared, is the same as x plus y, squared. A square doesn't care about the sign. So choice number one is always true, and it's out.
And there's a much simpler way to see it. Bars and an even power behave the same way. What's true with bars is true with a square.
Choice number two, let's leave it for the end.

Choice number three. The absolute value of x y, against the absolute value of x times the absolute value of y. Remember, you can split the bars over multiplication. So these two are always equal, never smaller. Never true, so it's out.
Choice number four. Inside the bars I have five x plus five y. Take out the common factor five, and it's five times x plus y. Then split the bars. That's five times the absolute value of x plus y.

So it says something is smaller than five times itself. That's true for every positive number. Could it fail? Only if x plus y were zero, but the given says it's more than three in absolute value. So it's always true, out.

Three are out, so in the exam you'd circle choice number two. Here, let's see why it's right. The rule from the lesson says the absolute value of a sum is smaller than or equal to the sum of the absolute values. They're equal when x and y have the same sign, and it's smaller when the signs are opposite. So sometimes true, sometimes not. Choice number two is our answer.

[pause] Our second method, plugging in numbers. I'll try one pair with the same sign and one with opposite signs, because signs are what the bars care about. First, x four and y one, small and easy. Four plus one is five, and five is bigger than three, so they fit the given.

Choice number one, five squared is twenty-five, and twenty-five is bigger than nine, true. Choice number two, the absolute value of four plus one is five, and four plus one is also five. Five smaller than five? No. Choice number three, four times one is four, in bars four, and four times one is four. Four smaller than four? No. Choice number four, five times five is twenty-five, and five is smaller than twenty-five, true.

Now opposite signs. Why x six and y negative two? Because with opposite signs they cancel, so I need one of them much bigger, to keep the sum above three. Six plus negative two is four, and four is bigger than three, so they fit.

Choice number one, four squared is sixteen, bigger than nine, true. Choice number two, the absolute value of six is six, and of negative two it's two, so six plus two is eight. Four smaller than eight? True this time. Choice number three, six times negative two is negative twelve, in bars twelve, and six times two is twelve. Twelve smaller than twelve? No again. Choice number four, five times four is twenty, and four is smaller than twenty, true.

So choice number two was false once and true once. That's exactly possible but not necessarily. Choice number three was never true, and choice numbers one and four were true both times. Choice number two.
Which way is better? If you know the rules, you can mark this one in seconds. If not, two pairs, same sign and opposite signs, will get you there. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
